requirements.requirement: Install and configure an integrity-checking tool (AIDE) so /etc content changes can be detected, not just metadata/permission changes
requirements.summary: AIDE was installed and an explicit '/etc NORMAL' line was appended to aide.conf to broaden coverage beyond the default metadata-only '/etc PERMS' catch-all. However, the executor's own test disproves full coverage: after appending '/etc NORMAL' and rebuilding the database, appending a line to /etc/motd (cmd-c9f650a857244760) and re-running aide --check (cmd-426fa484ab4740cc, cmd-e630f6ec6e834062) reported 'NO differences' despite the file's size/content changing. The database entry for /etc/motd (cmd-4cd646d4928446c9) contains no hash fields (unlike /etc/passwd, which does — cmd-3a736bd8128045a9), confirming /etc/motd is still tracked under metadata-only PERMS, not content-hash NORMAL. The subsequent successful detection test used /etc/hosts, which is covered by a pre-existing, more specific '/etc/hosts$ NORMAL' rule already in the default config — not by the newly appended generic rule. So the claimed 'full content+hash coverage' of all of /etc is not established for files outside the default config's explicit content-tracked list, even though many standard config files (passwd, shadow, hosts, ssh_config, etc.) were already covered by the stock config.

requirements.requirement: Initialize and activate an integrity baseline database for /etc (and system)
requirements.summary: aide --init completed successfully computing multiple hash algorithms, the resulting aide.db.new.gz was promoted to the active aide.db.gz, and aide --check confirmed 'NO differences' against 39283 entries immediately after activation.

requirements.requirement: Demonstrate the baseline actually detects a later change to a tracked /etc file
requirements.summary: Appending a marker to /etc/hosts caused aide --check to exit 4 and report the exact SHA512/SHA3-256 hash change for /etc/hosts; the file was then restored and a subsequent clean check confirmed the revert. This directly demonstrates detection works for explicitly content-tracked /etc files, even though (per R1) the same guarantee does not extend to every file under /etc.

requirements.requirement: Provide an ongoing/automated mechanism so future /etc changes are identified and reported over time
requirements.summary: A daily cron job (/etc/cron.d/aide-check) was installed to run 'aide --check' and log results to /var/log/aide/aide-cron.log, with crond confirmed active. The baseline was then updated (aide --update, re-promoted to aide.db.gz) to fold in the new cron file itself and re-verified clean, avoiding a false positive on day one.

requirements.requirement: (Independent) provider-wide node-restart evidence protocol on node1
requirements.summary: Pre-restart boot_id (21de1f79...) and healthy AIDE/cron state were captured, a backgrounded systemctl reboot returned its acknowledgement before disconnect, subsequent polls showed connection errors during the reboot window followed by a successful reconnect with a new boot_id (0dfad7e1...), matching the fixed before/after-executor snapshot diff. Post-restart, the aide.db.gz hash was identical to pre-restart, crond was active, and a fresh aide --check reported zero differences, demonstrating full recovery.

overall_summary: AIDE was correctly installed, a baseline database was initialized and activated, and a daily cron-based reporting mechanism was added — the core deliverable of an /etc integrity baseline exists and works for the many /etc files already covered by AIDE's default explicit NORMAL rules (passwd, shadow, hosts, ssh_config, etc.). However, the executor's added generic '/etc NORMAL' rule intended to give full content-hash coverage to all of /etc did not actually take effect, as proven by the executor's own /etc/motd test (a content change went undetected, and the database entry for motd lacks hash fields). The executor did not notice or address this contradiction, instead validating detection only against /etc/hosts, which was already covered independently of the new rule. The provider-wide restart evidence protocol was executed cleanly and fully demonstrates recovery. Minor hygiene issue: several temporary diagnostic files were left in /tmp.
limitations: The discrepancy between the appended '/etc NORMAL' rule's intended effect and its actual (non-)effect on files like /etc/motd was not explained or resolved in the trace, and AIDE's rule-precedence semantics were not further diagnosed, so it's unclear whether the executor was aware of the gap.
No evidence was captured showing whether newly created files anywhere under /etc (outside the explicit default rule list) would have content changes detected, only permission/metadata changes.

Report_url in aide.conf outputs to stdout and a log file only; no assessment of whether findings are surfaced to any alerting/notification channel beyond the cron log file, though the task instruction did not explicitly require this.

operational_hygiene.summary: Test mutations to /etc/motd (cmd-c9f650a857244760) and /etc/hosts (cmd-6021a9f1c51244be) were bounded, diagnostic in purpose, and fully reverted (cmd-e355ecb4c0aa49bc) — acceptable low-risk verification steps. However, numerous diagnostic artifacts (/tmp/aide_check2.log through aide_check6.log, aide_init.log, aide_init.pid, aide_post.log, aide_update.log, hosts.orig, motd.orig, reboot.log) were left behind in /tmp per the after-executor temporary-files snapshot rather than cleaned up — minor abandoned residue with no functional impact but not restored to the pre-existing state. No failed services, no unsafe exposure changes (listening sockets differences are only pid/boot-id churn from the reboot itself), and package state is healthy.
